newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore's Steamers Maritime to be telecom player.
newsitem.headline: Singapore's Steamers Maritime to be telecom player.

text.p: Singapore's Steamers Maritime Ltd, a unit of Keppel Corporation, is being transformed from a sleepy shipping and logistics company into a telecommunications concern, analysts said on Wednesday.
In the long-term, the move will be a boost for the firm, which is suffering from a downturn in the shipping sector, they said.

Steamers, soon to be renamed Keppel Telecommunications and Transportation Ltd, has a 21 percent stake in MobileOne (M1), Singapore's second mobile phone operator which should begin commercial operations next April.
Steamers' share price has started to rise ahead of MobileOne's April launch, hitting a new high of Singapore $1.48 ($1.05) on Wednesday, up 25 percent from the start of the year.

"The publicity generated by the launch of MobileOne come April should have a positive impact on Steamers' share price," said Sim Chey Hoon, vice president of corporate strategy and research group at Merrill Lynch Singapore.
She said M1, being the first and only cellular competitor to Singapore Telecom (SingTel), should draw significant public and market interest.
"Looking at the experience in other countries where a new operator comes in the market, all the enthusiasm is warranted," said David Leow, investment analyst with HSBC James Capel.
Leow said he expected MI, as well as SingTel, to step up marketing and advertising for their respective mobile phone services over the coming weeks.
"SingTel will be slightly hurt but not too much. There is going to be so much hype on mobile phones by April...we expect to see 40 percent growth in the market this year," said Leow.
SingTel should benefit from the growth unless average handphone rates come down by more than 20 percent, said Leow, who expects rates to come down by about 15 percent with the entry of MI.

Analysts expected M1, a consortium which includes Cable & Wireless, Hong Kong Telecom and Singapore Press Holdings Ltd, to grab at least 20 to 30 percent of the handphone market from SingTel over the next couple of years.
M1's mobile licence is valued by most analysts at around S$500 million a year. But the operator is not expected to make profits this year because of high start-up costs.
Steamers, which is expected to unveil disappointing 1996 results due to the doldrums in the shipping industry, may not see any positive contributions from M1 until 1998 or 1999, analysts said.

"In about six weeks, Steamers' results will be out and it would most likely disappoint. This year is going to see a fall in earnings because of the start-up costs and we expect MobileOne to break even only after 24 months," said Leow.
Analysts' concensus forecast according to The Estimate Directory put Steamers' 1996 net profit at S$14.4 million, up from last year's S$12.7 million.
But investors who are buying the stock have discounted Steamers' weak performance over the medium term, said analysts.

"Steamers used to be in the shipping business which is a low market rating industry. But now it is going into telecoms which has a much higher market rating," said an analyst with a foreign brokerage.
"It is a bit of a concept stock. You know it is going to make money but you are not sure about when the money will come in and how much," said Leow.
